_readme: State profile for tools/generate_location_pages.py. Schema: code (two capital letters, must equal the file name), name (state name used in copy), regions (object; each region key maps to: label = phrase used in headings and copy, e.g. 'northern Indiana'; counties = list of county names exactly as spelled in data/us-counties.json; climate = list of one or more climate paragraphs, each containing the {county} placeholder, one is chosen per page). Every county in data/us-counties.json for the state must appear in exactly one region. Optional county_content: {County: {trade: plain text}} (trade is roofing, siding, gutters or windows; PLAIN TEXT ONLY: no <, >, &, braces, backslashes or invisible/format characters; separate paragraphs with a blank line). Optional county_sources: {County: {trade: [{"label": plain text, "url": absolute https URL}, ...]}}, rendered as the page's Sources list; list only sources the county_content text cites, each URL fetched and confirmed to resolve, no duplicates. The CLI refuses a page that has county notes but no Sources list. A page is generated only if it has at least 500 words that appear on no other page in the run. Copy rules: the page lint bans have-contractors phrasing, 'vetted', vendor names and response-time claims. Every climate or weather statement names the public source it comes from and is worded as that source words it. Optional cities (gh-3600): {City: {"county": parent county}}; the parent must be a county listed in a region, and the city page takes its climate region and region sources from it. A city page is built at /locations/<city>-city-<state code>/<trade>/ from the same template as a county page. Optional city_content: {City: {trade: plain text}} and city_sources: {City: {trade: [{"label", "url"}, ...]}} (a city source may also carry an unrendered plain-text "note"), with the same rules as county_content and county_sources. Only (city, trade) pairs that have city_content are built, and each runs through the same 500-word strict-unique gate as the county pages in the same run.
name: Indiana

northern.label: northern Indiana
climate: {county} County is in the northern part of Indiana. NOAA's 2022 Indiana State Climate Summary says that in northwestern Indiana Lake Michigan moderates temperature, producing cooler summers and warmer winters, and that the lake is also the source of lake-effect snows, which can extend as far inland as Elkhart. It reports that some northern locations near Lake Michigan average more than 70 inches of snow a year, while the southwest averages about 14 inches.

NOAA's 2022 Indiana State Climate Summary gives annual precipitation as ranging from about 47 inches in the south of the state to 37 inches in the north, and says snowfall follows the reverse pattern. {county} County is in the northern part of Indiana, the end of that range with less precipitation. For snowfall the summary gives about 14 inches a year in the southwest and more than 70 inches in some northern locations near Lake Michigan. The same summary recounts a lake-effect storm on January 21 and 22, 2014 that dropped 18 inches of snow in Gary over a 5-hour period.

{county} County sits in northern Indiana. NOAA's 2022 Indiana State Climate Summary says the state's location in the interior of North America, with no mountains to the north or south, exposes it to bitterly cold Arctic air masses in winter and warm, humid air masses from the Gulf of Mexico in summer. It adds that dangerous storms can occur in every season: winter can bring snow and ice storms, and thunderstorms capable of producing floods, hail and tornadoes are common in the warmer months.

central.label: central Indiana
climate: {county} County sits in central Indiana. NOAA's 2022 Indiana State Climate Summary says dangerous storms can occur in every season, that winter can bring snow and ice storms, and that thunderstorms capable of producing floods, hail and tornadoes are common in the warmer months. It records that heavy snowstorms during the first week of January 2014 dropped 1 to more than 2 feet of snow over central and northern Indiana.

In central Indiana, where {county} County is located, NOAA's 2022 Indiana State Climate Summary notes that the state has a long and deadly history of tornadic storms. It identifies June 2, 1990 as Indiana's largest tornado outbreak, with 37 tornadoes, several of them at F4 intensity, and says spring and summer precipitation has generally been above average since the 1990s.

NOAA's 2022 Indiana State Climate Summary says annual average temperature varies by about 10 degrees F from north to south, that temperatures in Indiana have risen almost 1.5 degrees F since the beginning of the 20th century, and that the warming has been concentrated in winter and spring. It also says annual precipitation has been above average since 1990. {county} County is in central Indiana.

southern.label: southern Indiana
climate: {county} County lies in southern Indiana. NOAA's 2022 Indiana State Climate Summary puts annual precipitation at about 47 inches in the south of the state, against about 37 inches in the north, and says the southwest averages about 14 inches of snow a year.

{county} County is in southern Indiana. NOAA's 2022 Indiana State Climate Summary recounts a winter storm on December 22 and 23, 2004 that dropped more than 20 inches of snow across the southern part of the state, with 32 inches in the city of Washington. It says the snow lingered for several days and that a state of emergency was declared for 50 counties.

In southern Indiana, where {county} County lies, NOAA's 2022 Indiana State Climate Summary notes that the Tri-State Tornado of March 18, 1925 struck southwestern Indiana and destroyed parts of Griffin, Owensville and Princeton. The summary also reports that the 2012 drought caused major damage to crops, particularly in the southern third of the state.

Marion.roofing:
Hail, wind and tornado entries in NOAA's file

Open the Storm Events bulk files that NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information publishes for 2016 through 2026, keep the rows filed under Marion County, Indiana, and the result is 260 entries dated February 2016 through June 2026. Hail accounts for 66 of them, on 34 separate days. Forty-four of the hail entries, on 21 of those days, give a stone diameter of 1.00 inch or more. The two largest figures are 2.00 inches, one filed under Wanamaker on May 1, 2016 and one under Castleton on June 18, 2021. That June evening also carries two 1.75-inch entries, filed under Oaklandon and Five Points. The 2026 file used here is the one NOAA created on September 18, 2026; NOAA says it updates the current year's file each month, so the 2026 counts can change. The counts here leave out 48 more rows that NOAA files under forecast zones named Marion, such as High Wind and winter weather entries.

Hail in this file is not confined to the summer months. March holds more hail entries than any other month, 20 of them on 7 days, and 8 of the 20 share one date: March 27, 2016. NOAA's episode narrative for that date says thunderstorms developed "in warm and unstable air ahead of a cold front during the afternoon of Easter." The largest stones that day, 1.50 inches, are filed under Beech Grove and Homecroft, and the Homecroft entry reads "Ping pong sized hail was observed near Southport High School." After March come July with 12 entries on 6 days, then May and June with 11 each.

The wind entries outnumber the hail entries. NOAA files 152 thunderstorm wind entries for the county on 66 days; 39 of them give a measured gust and the other 113 an estimated one. June has the most, 38 entries on 12 days, followed by April with 25 and August with 23. June 18, 2025 is the busiest date at 14 entries, ahead of June 15, 2016 at 9 and both May 16, 2019 and April 2, 2025 at 8. Counted by year, 2025 is heaviest for wind, with 31 entries on 8 days. The highest thunderstorm gust in the county's file belongs to April 19, 2025: "An 84 mph thunderstorm wind gust was measured at the IND ASOS," which the episode narrative calls "the second strongest wind gust on record for the station."

What the wind did to buildings shows up in a handful of narratives. One places a roof blown off in the Sunshine Gardens area on April 8, 2020. Another, dated April 17, 2024, reads "Roof damage caused by thunderstorm wind gusts reported across Lawrence." On August 1, 2022 an entry describes five homes damaged by fallen trees and limbs in the Heatherwood Estates subdivision, and says some of those trees "went through the roofs." A May 16, 2019 entry from Mickleyville records "damage to siding of a home along the peak of the roof line," and an entry from Speedway on July 27, 2020 says two windows and a window frame were blown in. The newest roof reference is June 11, 2026, from the Acton area: "roof damage on Knapp and Mitthoeffer Roads."

Only three tornado entries sit in the file, on two days. An EF0 filed under Woodruff Place on August 24, 2016 blew windows out of a home near 25th and LaSalle Streets, and a building on Stanton Street sustained roof damage. On June 15, 2019 an EF1 began southwest of Beech Grove with winds NOAA puts at 100 mph; the narrative lists roof damage to a school, an apartment complex and a house, and says more than 20 classrooms at Beech Grove High School were damaged or destroyed. An EF0 near Five Points the same evening damaged outbuildings.

These are entries, not storms. A single afternoon can produce a dozen or more of them, and an entry exists only where someone reported or measured something. A quiet stretch in the file says nothing about whether a particular roof was struck, and an entry from a neighborhood a few miles away says little about the roof over your head. The counts above are this page's tally of the rows.

Housing stock

The Census Bureau's American Community Survey 5-year estimates for 2020 to 2024, table DP04, count 441,040 housing units in Marion County, 400,432 of them occupied. Owners live in 226,441 of the occupied units (56.5 percent) and renters in 173,991 (43.5 percent). Detached single-unit houses are the most common type at 261,039 units (59.2 percent), and buildings with 20 or more units hold 38,715 (8.8 percent).

By year built, the table places 66,271 units (15.0 percent) in 1939 or earlier, 25,337 in the 1940s, 53,751 in the 1950s, 59,103 in the 1960s and 54,891 in the 1970s. Those five bands add up to 259,353 units, or 58.8 percent of the total, built before 1980. The 1960s is the largest single-decade band at 13.4 percent. At the other end, 29,069 units (6.6 percent) date from 2010 to 2019. A house's build year is not its roof's age, since roofs get replaced, so ask when yours was last redone and whether paperwork exists.

Permits and local rules

The Department of Business and Neighborhood Services for the City of Indianapolis and Marion County publishes a Homeowner's Building Permit Guide. The copy read for this page carries no revision date. It says the department "is located at 1200 S Madison Ave, Indianapolis, Suite 100," directs residential permit questions to (317) 327-8700, and states: "Any construction requiring a building permit also requires that the applicant either be a licensed contractor in Marion county, or the property owner."

On roofs the guide speaks in two places. Under Common Projects it says: "Re-roofing and replacing siding will require a permit." It adds that a re-roofing permit may be obtained online through its Citizen's Access Portal or in person at the department. Under Work Exempt from Structural Permitting it lists "Replacement of an existing roof, if performed by a listed contractor that complies with the notice and posting requirements of section 536-216," unless the work changes the roof configuration, changes the covering in a way that would "increase the dead load," replaces the framing that supports the roof, "(e.g., replacement of a rafter or more than 128 feet of decking)," or uses "heat-applied roofing material." The same list adds that an owner-occupant "may affix without permit a layer of replacement shingles to a single layer of existing shingles" on stated conditions, and it warns that "an Improvement Location Permit could be required depending on scope." The guide does not say how the exemption relates to the re-roofing permit passage, so ask the department which applies at your address.

Its Adopted Codes section lists a "2020 International Residential Code (IRC)" and prints a Table 301.2(1) for the city: ground snow load 20, wind speed 115 (MPH), weathering "Severe," frost line depth 30 inches, winter design temperature 2 degrees F, and "No" under ice shield underlayment required. The guide's introduction says its references "use the 2020 Indiana Residential Code." For hired work, the guide says "the contractor must pull all required permits using her or his license," so that "the homeowner is protected from any violations or fees."

Rules change at some city lines inside the county. Lawrence, which appears in the county's NOAA file, has its own Department of Public Works roofing handout. It says "Building permits are NOT required except under the following conditions," and the list includes "25% or more of the decking is being replace OR," "After a natural disaster OR," a change in roof configuration, and a change in the type of roof covering "that would increase the dead load on the structure." It also says "All contractors engaged in roofing work must be registered in the City of Lawrence" and limits new roofing over an existing roof to "a total of two layers." The handout calls itself "intended only as a guide," based in part on the 2020 Indiana Residential Code, so confirm with the department at 317-545-8787.

What to settle before you ask for bids

- Which office issues roof permits at your address: the Department of Business and Neighborhood Services, or the building office of a city such as Lawrence.

- Whether each written bid names who pulls the permit, since the guide says the party doing the work should.

- The date of the most recent storm to reach your street, with photos taken afterward.

- The year your roof was last replaced, if any record exists.

Lake.roofing:
Wind first, then hail and tornadoes, in NOAA's northwest Indiana entries

NOAA's Storm Events bulk files for 2016 through 2026 hold 268 entries filed under Lake County, Indiana, running from June 2016 to June 2026. Wind dominates the file: 164 thunderstorm wind entries on 56 days, against 28 hail entries on 18 days and 22 tornado entries on 12 days. Of the wind entries, 36 give a measured gust and 128 an estimated one. March is the leading month for wind with 43 entries on 6 days, ahead of July with 36 on 12 days, June with 31 on 14 days, May with 24 on 9 days and August with 22 on 8 days. Counted by year, 2025 leads with 46 entries on 9 days. The 2026 file used here is the one NOAA created on September 18, 2026; NOAA says it updates the current year's file each month, so the 2026 counts can change. The counts here leave out 97 more rows that NOAA files under forecast zones named Lake, such as High Wind and winter weather entries.

A few dates account for much of the total. July 15, 2024 and March 30, 2025 each carry 12 wind entries, March 19, 2025 carries 11 and March 15, 2025 carries 10.

The narratives name two derechos. For August 10, 2020, NOAA writes that a line of intense thunderstorms known as a derecho "brought widespread severe wind damage across Iowa, northern Illinois and northern Indiana," and the same narrative reports that in northwest Indiana the winds downed a very large number of trees and damaged homes and other buildings. For July 15, 2024 the narrative opens: "A derecho moved across northwest Indiana during the evening of July 15th producing widespread wind damage and three tornadoes, one of which started in northeast Illinois."

Individual entries tie the wind to rooftops. On June 10, 2020 a Dyer entry says "Roof damage was reported to a residential structure near Calumet Avenue and 213th Street." On July 28, 2023 a Munster entry reads "Sections of a roof were blown off of a home on Timrick Drive in Munster." Two entries from Cedar Lake on March 15, 2025 say "Roofing and siding damage occurred around the neighborhood north of Hanover Central High School" and "Clay roofing tiles were ripped off of a church along 133rd Ave in Cedar Lake." Fifteen days later, a March 30, 2025 entry notes that "Shingles were damaged on a house in the Latitude subdivision in Winfield."

Hail is a smaller part of the file than wind. Twenty-five of the 28 hail entries give a diameter of 1.00 inch or more, and every one of the 18 hail days has at least one such entry. The largest figures are 1.75 inches, filed under St. John on July 7, 2017 and Dyer on June 10, 2020; three more entries sit at 1.50 inches. March has the most hail entries by month, 9 on 5 days, and no entry anywhere in the file reaches 2.00 inches.

The file's first tornado entry for the county is dated March 14, 2019, and 12 of the 22 are dated 2025 or 2026. Of the 22, fifteen are rated EF0, five EF1, one EF2 and one EF3. NOAA's narrative for the EF1 of March 31, 2023, which began in Merrillville, says it "blew out windows and tore sections of roofs off of multiple homes." A December 10, 2021 EF0 that ran from Cedar Lake toward Crown Point is described as producing "scattered light to moderate roof damage." Of March 19, 2025, when four tornadoes are filed, one in Gary "ripped off the roofs of several homes on west 21st Avenue." A July 15, 2024 EF1 that crossed in from Will County, Illinois, is described with "Numerous shingles were removed from a house on 121st Avenue" and "a house suffered significant siding damage" on 120th Avenue.

Five tornado entries share June 11, 2026. The EF2 filed under Lottaville moved through central Merrillville with estimated peak winds of 120 mph, and NOAA's narrative closes with the sentence: "At least 200 buildings and houses were damaged with over 60 houses suffering major damage." An EF0 the same day in Cedar Lake caused "roofing and siding damage to multiple houses," and an EF3 with estimated winds of 165 mph moved through rural parts of the county, where the narrative describes tree and crop damage.

NOAA's Indiana state climate summary adds regional context. It says that in northwestern Indiana Lake Michigan moderates temperature and is "the source of lake-effect snows," and recounts that a January 21 to 22, 2014 lake effect storm "dropped 18 inches of snow in Gary over a 5-hour period." The summary also says some northern locations near the lake average more than 70 inches of snow a year, against about 14 inches in the southwest.

Housing stock

The Census Bureau's American Community Survey 5-year estimates for 2020 to 2024, table DP04, count 217,436 housing units in the county, 195,130 of them occupied. Owners occupy 139,856 units (71.7 percent) and renters 55,274 (28.3 percent). Detached single-unit houses are 154,940 units (71.3 percent).

By year built, the table places 31,748 units (14.6 percent) in 1939 or earlier, 19,974 in the 1940s, 33,515 in the 1950s, 28,459 in the 1960s and 29,726 in the 1970s. Together those bands make 143,422 units, or 66.0 percent, built before 1980, and the 1950s is the largest single-decade band at 15.4 percent. Only 14,854 units (6.8 percent) date from 2010 or later. Bring the date of your roof's last replacement to any conversation about its condition.

Permits and local rules

Lake County's Plan Commission publishes a "Procedure for Requesting a Building Permit" that gives 219-755-3700 for questions. Its licensing language refers to an "Unincorporated Licensing Board." It requires that applications "must be signed by the owner of the property or a contractor holding a CURRENT LAKE COUNTY CONTRACTOR'S LICENSE" and says contractors "shall be licensed per Contractor License Ordinance #1628." The procedure does not mention roofing.

Towns and cities set their own rules. Crown Point's Building Department answers the question in its FAQ: "No permit is needed if you're only re-roofing or re-shingling. A permit is required if you're replacing rafters or sheeting." Merrillville's building permit page lists new construction, additions, pools, sheds, fences, detached garages, decks, signs, and excavation and fill; re-roofing is not on that list, and the page says "Merrillville requires that all contractors be licensed with the Town." Hammond licenses by trade: its contractor license application, revised January 8, 2026, offers "Residential Roofing" and "Exterior Remodeling" as license types, with an open-book exam, a one-hour limit and a 70 percent passing score. None of these pages is a substitute for a call to the office that serves your street.

What to settle before you ask for bids

- Which jurisdiction your address falls in: the county Plan Commission, or the building office of your own town or city.

- Whether your town expects the work to be done by someone it licenses, and whether the written bids mention the permit question at all.

- The date of the most recent storm to reach your street, with photos taken afterward.

- The year your roof was last replaced, if any record exists.

Allen.roofing:
A short list of heavy storm dates in NOAA's file

Filter NOAA's Storm Events bulk files for 2016 through 2026 to Allen County, Indiana, and you get 238 entries, the first dated March 27, 2016 and the latest June 11, 2026. Thunderstorm wind makes up 156 of them, but they fall on only 39 days, so the county's wind history is concentrated on a small number of dates. Hail adds 63 entries on 25 days, tornadoes 5 entries on 4 days, and flooding 9 entries. Of the wind entries, 25 give a measured gust and 131 an estimated one. July holds 54 wind entries on 8 days, more than any other month, followed by March with 28 on 4 days, August with 25 on 6 days, June with 21 on 8 days and May with 20 on 8 days. The 2026 file used here is the one NOAA created on September 18, 2026; NOAA says it updates the current year's file each month, so the 2026 counts can change. The counts here leave out 51 more rows that NOAA files under forecast zones named Allen, such as High Wind and winter weather entries.

Two years stand out. NOAA files 42 wind entries on 6 days in 2022, and 31 on 6 days in 2020. The single busiest date is July 5, 2022 with 22 entries; the episode narrative says "Widespread wind damage occurred in an area from Steuben County through Allen County in Indiana." March 6, 2022 follows with 14. One entry that day reads "The ASOS at Fort Wayne International Airport recorded a 67 mph wind gust," and another says county dispatch received "reports of power flashes and tree damage across the entire county."

The hail entries are a different pattern: 41 of the 63, on 14 days, give 1.00 inch or more. Three entries read 2.00 inches, two filed under Georgetown on April 19, 2017 and one under Greendale on June 1, 2019. Three more read 1.75 inches: Royal Oaks on May 16, 2019 and again on July 23, 2022, and Huntertown on June 13, 2022. June 1, 2019 is the heaviest hail date at 10 entries; NOAA's narrative says surface CAPE values were "in excess of 3000 J/KG" and that thunderstorms "became prolific hail producers." Winter is not hail-free here. February holds 8 hail entries on 2 days, six of them on February 19, 2026, when the narrative notes that low freezing levels produced "efficient hail producing storms" and that one storm left "a swath of 1 to 2 inches of pea size or larger hail along its path."

What the entries say about buildings is mostly about shingles and trees. On March 1, 2017 an entry from Wallen reports that "the roof of a business was damaged as well as parts of the interior of the building." A May 19, 2019 entry from Aboite describes "shingles blown off roofs." On June 21, 2021, in Zulu, "A large pole barn had the entire metal roof ripped off and blown across the road towards the east," and debris from it struck two homes about 220 feet away. A February 27, 2023 entry from Westlawn says "A home sustained some shingle and siding damage," and a second from Cedar Canyons that day notes "some roof damage to a residence."

The five tornado entries include an EF3. It was recorded on August 24, 2016, and ran 5.16 miles from Milan Center to Georgetown. NOAA's narrative says "A poorly anchored home was wiped off its foundation," that a two-story barn was leveled, and that maximum winds were estimated at 160 mph. An EF2 on March 31, 2023 began on the northeast side of Fort Wayne at Maplewood Park and, in the narrative's words, "raced northeast toward the town of Harlan. Many homes and farms had minor to major damage." A brief EF0 formed near Harlan the same day. On August 20, 2016 an EF0 near Brookside Estates left "minor shingle damage" at one Eby Road residence, and an EF0 on July 29, 2023 crossed the county line from Whitley County and brought minor roof and siding damage to one home. The file does not say how many addresses lay along each path.

An entry is a report, not an inspection. The entries above cite spotters, members of the public, emergency managers and airport weather stations. The tallies in this section are the page's own counts of those rows.

Housing stock

The Census Bureau's American Community Survey 5-year estimates for 2020 to 2024, table DP04, count 166,285 housing units in the county, 156,570 of them occupied, an occupancy rate of 94.2 percent. Owners live in 107,825 occupied units (68.9 percent) and renters in 48,745 (31.1 percent). Detached single-unit houses are 121,951 units (73.3 percent) and mobile homes 4,685 (2.8 percent).

By year built, the table places 21,642 units (13.0 percent) in 1939 or earlier, 7,628 in the 1940s, 16,834 in the 1950s, 21,700 in the 1960s and 24,004 in the 1970s. Those bands total 91,808 units, or 55.2 percent, built before 1980. The 1970s is the largest decade band at 14.4 percent, followed by the 1960s at 13.0 percent and the 1990s at 12.9 percent. Newer construction is a real share too: 13,580 units (8.2 percent) date from 2010 to 2019 and 3,423 (2.1 percent) from 2020 or later.

Permits and local rules

The Allen County Building Department, at 200 E Berry St., Suite 180 in Fort Wayne, publishes a one-page Residential Permit Guide marked 03/04/2026. Its flowchart first asks whether you are adding or expanding a structure. If not, it asks: "Does the work involve any mechanical, electrical, plumbing, HVAC, or structural alteration?" Where the answer is yes, the list headed "PERMIT REQUIRED FOR" includes an item for roofing and siding, with one submittal item, a construction plan. Where the answer is no, the guide says "You do not need a permit from the Allen County Building Department," then adds that "Additional permits or approval may be required from another agency." The chart's pictures put roofing and siding on the yes side. The department's Introduction to Home Projects page is plainer: its list of "Examples of projects needing permits" begins with "Re-roofing" and includes "Replacing windows." Questions go to (260) 449-7131.

Licensing is addressed in the department's Rules and Regulations, nineteenth edition, effective 9/6/2024. Section A.7.b says an individual who contracts in "the improving, remodeling, and repair of existing one- and two-family structures shall be required to be licensed with the Building Department," and the sub-contractor list in A.8 includes a roofing category. The department's FAQ asks "Is my project in the Allen County jurisdiction?" and answers with a link to a jurisdiction map. Since November 7, 2025, permit applications for properties inside Fort Wayne's local historic districts follow a new process that the department says is meant to ensure consistent review of historic preservation requirements.

One more wrinkle concerns the codebook. The department's page lists an Indiana Residential Code based on the 2018 International Residential Code, effective December 26, 2019, and the page does not say whether a later edition has taken its place. Ask which edition applies to a project before you assume a detail.

What to settle before you ask for bids

- Whether your address sits in the department's jurisdiction map or in a town that issues its own permits.

- Whether the written bids say who obtains the permit and who calls for inspections.

- The date of the most recent storm to reach your street, with photos taken afterward.

- The year your roof was last replaced, and whether any record of that work exists.

Hamilton.roofing:
Storm reports NOAA holds for Hamilton County, Indiana

Hamilton County's hail history in NOAA's Storm Events Database comes to 52 reports spread over 22 separate days, the first on March 27, 2016 and the last on May 16, 2025. Thirty of the 52, covering 15 of those days, were an inch across or bigger. The calendar has two blanks: nothing was entered for 2019, and the 2026 file shows no hail at all. Seasonally, March dominates with 30 reports on seven dates; June comes next with seven reports (four dates), then April with six (four dates), July with four, May with three and August with two. Two years carry most of the weight: 2020 holds 15 reports on just two dates, and 2021 holds 11 on four.

The biggest stone on file measures 2.50 inches. It was entered at Sheridan on June 25, 2023, and the NOAA narrative for it says "Thunderstorm hail as large as tennis balls in and north of Sheridan." Three stones of 1.75 inches sit one step down: Atlanta (May 1, 2016), College Meadows (June 18, 2021) and Carmel (March 14, 2024). March 28, 2020 is the most crowded day in the hail record, with 12 reports scattered across Carmel, Noblesville, Fishers, Hortonville and Sheridan. Carmel and Noblesville supplied four each, and the two 1.50-inch reports on that date came from Fishers and Noblesville. The runner-up day is March 27, 2021, with six.

Thunderstorm wind is the larger file: 71 reports on 39 dates between June 20, 2016 and June 11, 2026, of which 62 carry an estimated-gust label and nine a measured one. May leads by month with 21 reports on six dates. Behind it: July with 12 (eight dates), August with 10 (six dates) and June with nine (five dates). The worst single day was May 16, 2019, with ten entries: Eagletown five, Fishers two, Carmel two and College Meadows one. In the September 18 build, 2019 and 2026 tie for busiest at 12 reports apiece, while 2016, 2018 and 2024 had two each. The 2026 file was built in September, so that year's count stops short of a full season.

NOAA's column guide gives wind speeds in knots. Hamilton's top reading is 74 knots, an estimate entered at Boxley on November 5, 2017, with the narrative "A roof of a barn and an old shed was destroyed." That 74 is a large outlier, since the next-highest Hamilton value is 61 knots. The highest measured gust is 61 knots, at Home Place on May 23, 2019, and a 60-knot measured gust followed on March 28, 2020. Two roof-related narratives are worth reading in full. On March 6, 2022, filed under Clarksville: "Thunderstorm winds blew many shingles off of roofs while bits of siding were ripped from houses." On May 19, 2026, filed under Noblesville: "Tree downed by thunderstorm winds onto a house and through the roof."

Hamilton is also the name of a forecast zone, and two more wind categories sit under that zone rather than under any town. High Wind has nine entries on eight dates, from April 2, 2016 through March 13, 2026. Strong Wind has three: March 29, 2020, November 15, 2020 and March 18, 2021. The first of those narratives describes several reports of small amounts of siding torn off by strong gradient winds.

Hamilton logged three tornadoes, each in a different year. An EF1 on August 15, 2016 near Boxley ran 0.42 miles and 100 yards wide. An EF0 on July 29, 2024 at Walnut Grove began with "damage to the roof of a metal barn and uprooted trees along Strawtown Road" and then skipped into Madison County. The April 2, 2025 EF1 ran 6.6 miles and 150 yards wide, from near 116th Street and Pennsylvania Street to 146th Street and Community Drive; its narrative says "numerous homes and apartment buildings sustaining roof and siding damage," with peak gusts of 105 mph.

On the forecasting side, weather.gov lists Hamilton County as code INC057 and puts it in the Indianapolis office's territory, abbreviated IND. NOAA built the 2026 file on September 18, 2026 and refreshes it monthly, which is why any 2026 figure here can still shift.

What the Census says about Hamilton County homes

The figures below come from DP04, the housing profile in the Census Bureau's American Community Survey, using the 2020 to 2024 estimates pooled over five years. It tallies 144,746 dwellings in Hamilton County. Of these, 137,252 have someone living in them and 7,494 are empty (5.2 percent). Homeowners occupy 104,416 of the lived-in dwellings (76.1 percent) and renters 32,836 (23.9 percent); the tenure shares are measured against occupied homes, while every other percentage is measured against all dwellings. Detached single-family houses account for 108,264 (74.8 percent), mobile homes for 2,118 (1.5 percent).

June supplies 28 rows over 15 dates; May 16 over 5; July 11 over 6; April and August 7 apiece, over 5 and 4 dates; October 6 over 2; March 5 over 3; and November 3 over 3.

The worst stretch is the last week of May 2019. May 23 has 5 rows, May 26 has 6 (Purdue University airport, Meadowbrook, Eastwich, Lafayette twice, Klondyke) and May 27 has 3, with a measured 72 mph gust at the Montmorencie airport. On May 26 the Meadowbrook narrative says "Siding and roof shingles were ripped off buildings." Elsewhere the roof-related rows are scattered: a gazebo destroyed at Lafayette on May 19, 2019; "A 24 by 20 foot metal pole barn was blown down" at Montmorencie on October 11, 2021, a 60-knot estimate; "A large amount of siding blown off a home" at Romney on March 30, 2025; and, at Octagon on March 31, 2023, 65 knots with "Thunderstorm winds flattened two structures to their basements" and "Roofs were blown off of several other structures near the junction of Benton, Tippecanoe and White Counties." Klondyke on June 18, 2025 records large branches falling onto "a car and townhomes."

Two measured gusts top the list, both on June 22, 2016. Cairo logged 87 knots with "A 100 mph thunderstorm wind gust was measured in this location," and North Crane logged 76 knots with "An 87 mph thunderstorm wind gust was measured in this location." Among estimates, the Halsmer airport label holds the highest at 70 knots on July 21, 2020. The airport station on the Purdue campus measured 65 knots on July 15, 2024, which its narrative gives as 75 mph.

Seven tornado rows cover six dates: two in 2016, then one apiece in 2017, 2018 and 2021, then a pair on June 18, 2025. Five are EF0 and two are EF1. The Meadowbrook EF1 of March 31, 2016 ran 0.14 miles at 30 yards wide with winds estimated near 100 mph, and its narrative notes "a guard shack was destroyed." At Cairo, an EF0 on August 15, 2016 followed a 0.51-mile track 40 yards wide. For the Dayton EF0 of November 18, 2017 (0.32 miles, 110 yards) the narrative says "A few strips of siding was removed from the house." On April 3, 2018 an EF0 filed at the Lafayette Aretz airport label, 0.64 miles by 40 yards, "affected one homestead and a thin band of trees." The Pettit EF1 on June 25, 2021 is entered here at 0.77 miles by 50 yards inside a 2.17-mile survey path that also crossed Carroll County; the survey notes "The roof on the east side of a barn was lifted and thrown about 20 yards to the southeast." The June 18, 2025 pair are both EF0: West Pt, 0.56 miles with a peak wind of 80 mph, and Klondyke, 0.34 miles at 75 mph with "minor roof damage to a home on 500N."

Notes on how these rows were counted

NOAA spreads the 112 rows over 33 place labels. Lafayette and the Purdue University airport label tie at 13, Klondyke has 7, Elston 6, and Battle Ground and Montmorencie 5 apiece. A label marks where a forecaster put a report, which can differ from the town a resident would name. Reports came from the public (41 rows), broadcast media (17), emergency managers (13), trained spotters (10), automated airport stations (7), and amateur radio operators and storm surveys (6 each); another 12 rows were filed by five less common kinds of observer. NOAA's format guide gives times in local standard time in most cases, so this page keeps to dates. Excluded from every count: 34 zone-based Tippecanoe rows (Heavy Snow 8, Drought 7, High Wind 6, Extreme Cold/Wind Chill 5, Winter Storm 4, and one apiece of Strong Wind, Winter Weather, Excessive Heat and Cold/Wind Chill), plus 4 county-level flooding rows, flood and flash flood together. NOAA dated the 2026 file October 26, 2026, and its README promises a monthly refresh of this year's data, so the newest Tippecanoe figures could still change.

Tippecanoe's weather zone and the roof table in the state code

Zone INC157 is Tippecanoe's code in Weather Service records, and its forecasts come from the IND office in Indianapolis. Indiana's amended copy of Table R301.2(1) is printed at the end of a guidance sheet from the state's homeland security department about drip edge and ice barriers on asphalt-shingled Class 2 homes. For Tippecanoe its row reads 115 mph wind, 20 psf snow load on the ground, 30 inches in the foundation column, seismic category A, and ice shield marked "No." In a "No" county the sheet leaves the layer to whatever the shingle manufacturer's written installation instructions say.

The age and makeup of Tippecanoe County's housing

Census Bureau survey estimates for 2020 to 2024 count 189,071 people and 80,647 dwellings, occupied or not, in Tippecanoe County. Occupied units total 75,808 and vacant ones 4,839 (6.0 percent). Owner households number 40,470 (53.4 percent of occupied) against 35,338 renter households (46.6 percent). Standalone single-family houses make up 47,272 units (58.6 percent), and mobile homes make up 1,997 (2.5 percent). Census gives 1987 as the median construction year (margin of error 2), meaning roughly half the county's units were standing by the end of 1987. Before 1980 came 34,489 units (42.8 percent); 1980 through 1999 added 19,179 (23.8 percent); 26,979 (33.5 percent) arrived in 2000 or later. The 2000s lead the decades with 14,224 units (17.6 percent), while 8,771 (10.9 percent) are from 1939 or earlier. All of this is sampled, each estimate carries a margin of error, and nothing in these tables says when a particular roof went on.

Which Tippecanoe County office handles your address

Permit counters differ by address. The Tippecanoe County Building Commission, 20 North 3rd Street in Lafayette, 765-423-9225, keeps weekday hours of 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM and lists a general building permit application among its downloads. Its FAQ answers "Where do I get a building permit?" by sending Lafayette addresses to 765-807-1050 and West Lafayette addresses to 765-775-5130, then adds "If you live outside any of these areas, you would be considered to be in the county." Roofing does not appear in that FAQ.

Lafayette's permit desk is part of Engineering and Public Works at 20 N 6th Street, which lists 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Its residential checklist states "The General Contractor will need a $5000 Bond" and requires city licensing for an electrician; the checklist and the permit page leave roofing unmentioned. West Lafayette's Margerum City Hall, 222 N Chauncey Ave, (765) 775-5130, open weekdays 8:00am to 4:30pm, runs a building permit FAQ with the entry "Do I need a reroofing permit?" and the answer "No, not unless any structural materials are being replaced." Battle Ground, Dayton and the other towns were not checked, and no countywide reroofing rule turned up.

Roofer licensing as the state describes it

Roofing is absent from the Professional Licensing Agency's profession list, which names home inspectors, plumbing and real estate among others. Indiana's Attorney General, writing about storm-chaser scams, advises asking your own building department whether a permit applies and says no contractor should begin before one is issued; licensing rules, the leaflet adds, change from one community to another. In Tippecanoe County that leaves the question with whichever office covers your street: Lafayette, West Lafayette, a town or the county.

Tippecanoe County bid checklist

- Pin down the office with authority over your address first: Lafayette, West Lafayette, another town, or the county Building Commission.

- Have each bidder say in writing whether the job needs a permit at your address, and how that answer changes if decking or other structural wood has to be replaced.

- Ask who files for the permit and who requests the inspection.

- The state table leaves Tippecanoe at "No" for ice shield, so have each bidder show you what the shingle brand's own installation sheet says about that layer.

- If a bidder is a general contractor, ask what bond or registration the office covering your address requires; Lafayette's checklist names a $5000 bond.

- Hand every bidder the same copy of any written estimate you hold from your insurer.

St. Joseph.roofing:
St. Joseph County, Indiana storm record, 2016 to 2026: hail, damaging gusts and tornadoes as NOAA logged them

NOAA's yearly Storm Events detail files for 2016 through 2026, cut down to rows filed under St. Joseph County, Indiana, leave 44 hail rows that fall on 12 distinct dates between February 24, 2017 and June 25, 2024. Hail here comes in bursts. 2017 brings 11 rows across 4 dates and 2019 brings 9 across 3. Then 2021 brings 4 rows on one date, 2022 brings 5 on one date, 2023 brings 14 across 2 dates, and 2024 brings a single row. No hail row is filed for 2016, 2018, 2020, 2025 or 2026. Sizes, as typed, are 0.75 inch on 14 rows, 0.88 on 5, 1.00 on 12, 1.25 on 3, 1.50 on 7, 1.75 on 1, 2.00 on 1 and 2.50 on 1, so an inch or more shows up on 25 rows across 9 dates.

Two days produce the three biggest stones. On July 20, 2023, nine rows are filed: four at Mishawaka (2.50 from a public report, 2.00, 1.50 and 1.00), three at South Bend (1.50, 1.00 and 1.00), plus Glenwood and Maple Lane at 1.50 each. The 2.00 narrative says "A two inch hail stone was measured near Marion High School," and the trained spotter at Maple Lane wrote "Golf ball size hail reported at the intersection of Ironwood and Mckinley." The 1.75 is Lakeville on March 31, 2023, a public report of "approximately golf ball sized hail at Lakeville High School" with "Several vehicles were damaged." Four other days carry five rows each: February 28, 2017 (topped by a 1.25 at Mishawaka), June 1, 2019 (two Gilmer Park rows at 1.25), June 13, 2022 (all five at Granger, none above 0.88) and March 31, 2023, the Lakeville day. Month by month, June has 17 rows over 5 dates, July 9 on one, February 7 over 2, March 6 over 2 and August 5 over 2. Because 14 of the 44 rows come from 2023 and 9 from a single afternoon, the hail total reflects how many people reported one storm more than how often hail strikes.

Wind makes up the bulk of the record, with 180 rows over 55 dates from March 24, 2016 to July 27, 2026. NOAA labels 169 as estimated gusts (EG) and 11 as measured gusts (MG), and none is below 50 knots. Counting rows and then dates, 2024 leads with 34 and 9, trailed by 2021 with 32 and 8. Next are 2019 and 2023 with 20 each, over 7 and 3 dates; 2016 and 2025 with 15 each, over 5 and 3; 2018 with 13 over 5; 2020 with 11 over 4; 2026 with 10 over 6; 2022 with 8 over 4; and 2017 with 2 on a single date. June has 46 rows over 13 dates. March has 30 over 7, May 28 over 8, July 28 over 9, August 23 over 9, September 16 over 6, October 7 on one date and April 2 over 2.

March 30, 2025 is the largest single day, with 12 rows, among them the two highest values in the file, both 70 knots. The Mishawaka narrative says "There is roof damage and significant shingle loss from a building at Smith and 8th." At Twin Branch Jct the report describes "Drone footage of eight power poles snapped or bent at the base." Granger's 61-knot row that day adds "Some instances of property damage, including shingles blown off a church." After that day come June 26, 2021 with 9 rows, July 5, 2023 with 8, and three days with 7 each: September 27, 2019, October 11, 2021 and March 31, 2023. The top measured gust, 69 knots at the Michiana airport label on July 5, 2023, is described: "The ASOS at the South Bend International Airport recorded a 79 mph wind gust." Other roof or siding rows include Gilmer Park on March 24, 2016 ("A roof was blown off a building on West Dunham"), Maple Lane on September 27, 2019 (60 knots, "some roof shingles blown off"), Pine on March 31, 2023 ("Shingles were ripped off a roof"), Mishawaka on July 15, 2024 (65 knots, "Loss of siding to a home in Mishawaka") and Indian Vlg on September 24, 2024 ("One residence sustained roof damage"). South Bend on June 18, 2025 has a minor siding report for a home on the city's south side.

Tornado rows number nine and cover seven dates. Two fall on October 12, 2016 and two on June 23, 2019; five other dates carry one apiece. NOAA rates six EF0, two EF1 and one EFU, a code that is not among the EF0 to EF5 examples in NOAA's format guide. On October 12, 2016 the Gilmer Park EF0 ran 1.25 miles at 30 yards wide, while the South Bend EF0 covered 0.05 miles. On June 23, 2019 the Woodland EF0, 0.48 miles at 10 yards wide, destroyed an outdoor structure while "removing siding and shingles from a detached garage," and the Nutwood EF0 went 2.01 miles at 250 yards wide. The Wyatt EF1 of August 10, 2020 followed 2.41 miles at 100 yards, with winds estimated at 110 mph; grain bins were toppled and farm outbuildings damaged. At Woodland on June 21, 2021 an EF1 of 1.05 miles at 100 yards is the row where "a barn lost its roof." The Hamilton EFU of October 3, 2021 spans 0.01 miles and reports "No damage was reported." Last in the list are an EF0 at Indian Vlg on September 24, 2024 (0.29 miles, estimated 70 mph) and an EF0 on April 17, 2026 under the Michiana airport label (1.28 miles at 200 yards, estimated 80 mph) whose narrative attributes "the majority of any structure damage" to falling trees.

Notes on the St. Joseph counts

NOAA applies 31 place labels to the 233 rows. South Bend has 38 and Mishawaka 33; the Michiana airport label and Granger have 15 apiece, and Glenwood and Nutwood 14 apiece. Labels show where a forecaster placed a report, which a homeowner may not call by the same name. By source, the public contributed 100 rows, broadcast media 44, trained spotters 34, fire and rescue departments 11, amateur radio operators 10, state officials 9, storm surveys 8 and automated airport stations 7; 10 more come from five other kinds of observer. NOAA's format guide gives times in local standard time in most cases, so only dates are printed here. Not counted are 41 rows typed as forecast zones named St. Joseph (Winter Weather 21, Winter Storm 7, Lake-Effect Snow 5, High Wind 4, Heavy Snow 2, Extreme Cold/Wind Chill 1 and Dense Fog 1), plus these county rows: 11 for flood or flash flood, 3 for lightning and 3 for heavy rain. NOAA stamped the 2026 file October 26, 2026 and refreshes the current year monthly, so newer counts may differ.

Forecast zone and the roof table: the St. Joseph entry

Weather Service maps put St. Joseph County in zone INC141 and hand its forecasts to the Northern Indiana office (IWX); Morgan and Tippecanoe, by contrast, fall to Indianapolis (IND). The St. Joseph row of Table R301.2(1), in the amended Indiana version appended to Indiana Homeland Security guidance covering eave protection and drip edge for shingled Class 2 houses, reads 115 mph design wind, 30 psf of snow, 36 inches of foundation depth, Seismic Design Category A and a "Yes" in the ice shield column. The Tippecanoe line reads "No" in that column. The sheet says some counties are ones where ice and water shield is "always required" under the table, and a "Yes" row puts St. Joseph among them.

Housing in St. Joseph County and when it went up

The 2020 to 2024 American Community Survey gives St. Joseph County 273,040 residents and 118,580 housing units. Occupied units come to 107,252 and vacant units to 11,328 (9.6 percent). Owner-occupied homes number 74,022 (69.0 percent of occupied units) and rentals 33,230 (31.0 percent). Single-family houses standing alone account for 87,530 units (73.8 percent), and mobile homes for 1,873 (1.6 percent). The Census median for year built lands on 1968 (margin of error 1), which puts roughly half of St. Joseph County's units at 1968 or older. Counting every unit, 76,339 (64.4 percent) were built before 1980; the 1980s and 1990s account for 23,552 (19.9 percent), and 2000 and after for 18,689 (15.8 percent). The 1950s lead the decades with 16,825 units (14.2 percent), and the biggest age group of all is 1939 or earlier at 22,830 (19.3 percent). These are survey estimates with margins of error, and no table says when a roof was last replaced.

The offices that issue roofing permits in St. Joseph County

One department covers much of the county. The Building Department, which its county roofing form heads with both St. Joseph County and the City of South Bend, is at 125 S Lafayette Blvd, Suite 100, South Bend, phone 574-235-9554. Its residential permitting guide lists "Remodeling worth more than $500 including roofing, siding, windows/doors, and interior remodeling" among work that needs a permit and says "Work requiring permits also requires a registered contractor." The guide has the department handling the city, "All 5 digit County addresses" and, after Town Board approval, the towns of Lakeville, Roseland, Indian Village, North Liberty and Osceola. It says it does not cover four-digit-or-shorter addresses in Mishawaka, New Carlisle or Walkerton.

That department also publishes a "County Residential Roofing Permit Application" with a cost line reading "TEAR-OFF/RE-ROOF: $ OR OVERLAY: $". The form warns "If work has been started without a permit, you will be triple fined" and states "Receipt of application does not mean a permit has been issued." It allows 6 months from issuance to start the work and 2 years to finish it, and a missed deadline means reapplying. Mishawaka's Building Department, 100 Lincolnway West, (574) 258-1607, open weekdays from 7:30 am to 4:45 pm, says it "handles contractor licenses and building permits"; its page does not mention roofing. New Carlisle and Walkerton were not checked.

Roofer licensing: what the state publishes

Roofing is not on the Indiana Professional Licensing Agency's profession list, which includes home inspectors, plumbing and real estate. A consumer leaflet from Indiana's Attorney General sends readers to their building office to learn whether a permit is needed, and to their city or county for licensing rules where they live. In St. Joseph County the practical answer comes from whichever of the South Bend department, Mishawaka or a town office covers your address.

Questions to settle before you sign a St. Joseph County bid

- Identify the office that covers your address: the South Bend department (city, 5-digit county addresses and some towns), Mishawaka, New Carlisle, Walkerton or a town.

- Have each bidder say whether the job is a tear-off or an overlay and put that in the written bid, because the county application has a cost line for each.

- Confirm each bidder holds a contractor registration with whichever office issues your permit, because the South Bend department's guide ties permit work to registered contractors.

- Find where ice and water shield appears in the written bid, because the state table lists "Yes" for St. Joseph.

- Ask the bidder to confirm the permit has been issued before work starts, since an application receipt is not a permit.

- Hand every bidder the same copy of any written estimate you hold from your insurer.

Carmel, Indiana: hail, wind and one tornado in NOAA's storm files, 2016 to 2026

NOAA's Storm Events detail files for 2016 through 2026 list every Carmel report under Hamilton County, never under the city, so this page assigns each entry to a city by its map point. Of the 128 hail, thunderstorm wind and tornado entries filed under Hamilton County, the Census Bureau's geocoder places 40 inside the city of Carmel: 18 hail entries on 11 dates, 21 thunderstorm wind entries on 15 dates and one tornado. Hail first appears on August 26, 2016 (07:35 EST, 08:35 daylight time) and last on May 16, 2025. By year, entries then dates, the hail list reads 2016 with 1 and 1, 2017 with 2 and 1, 2018 with 1 and 1, 2020 with 6 and 2, 2021 with 6 and 4, 2024 with 1 and 1, and 2025 with 1 and 1. No Carmel hail is filed for 2019, 2022, 2023 or 2026.

Reported stone sizes in inches, with entry counts, are 0.75 (7), 0.88 (1), 1.00 (7), 1.25 (1), 1.50 (1) and 1.75 (1), so 10 entries on 6 dates reach one inch. March holds 8 hail entries on 4 dates, June 4 on 2, April 3 on 2, May 2 on 2 and August 1. The busiest hail day is March 28, 2020 with four entries, the largest a 1.50 typed under a Fishers label and relayed through Twitter. A label is the spot a forecaster typed, not a boundary, and the 19 here carry only three: Eagletown 12, Hortonville 4 and Carmel 3. By source, NOAA credits the public with 11, trained spotters 3, emergency managers 2, and one each an amateur radio operator, law enforcement and social media. NOAA's format guide gives its times as "usually in LST", meaning local standard time. Westfield's entries are stamped EST, so all 19 get an hour added for daylight time. Entries for event types other than these three are not counted. This page reads the 2026 file as NOAA stamped it on October 26, 2026; the README says the current year's file is updated each month, which means recent counts can move.

The forecast zone and the state's roofing rule

The National Weather Service record for Hamilton County is zone INC057, with the Indianapolis office (IND) as its forecast office. In the Indiana Department of Homeland Security sheet titled "Ice and Water Shield Update 2020-02-25", the amended Table R301.2(1) row for Hamilton shows 115 mph, Seismic Design Category A and 20 psf of ground snow, with "No" under Ice Shield Underlayment Required. The sheet says roof coverings "shall be applied in accordance with the applicable provisions of this section and the manufacturer's installation instructions."

Westfield houses and their ages

Westfield city has 22,030 housing units in the Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 American Community Survey housing profile, table DP04. Of these, 20,984 are occupied and 1,046 vacant (4.7 percent). Owners live in 16,681 of the occupied units (79.5 percent) and renters in 4,303 (20.5 percent). Detached houses total 17,149 (77.8 percent) and mobile homes 304 (1.4 percent). Table B25035 gives a median year built of 2010, margin of error 1. Westfield's housing stock is younger than that of Carmel, Fishers or Noblesville: 16,032 units (72.8 percent) were built in 2000 or later, 4,342 (19.7 percent) from 1980 through 1999 and only 1,656 (7.5 percent) before 1980. The 2010s are the largest decade at 8,115 units (36.8 percent), and 2,848 units (12.9 percent) date from 2020 or later. Roof replacement dates are not in either table, which count houses.

Who issues permits in Westfield

The city's offices, at 2728 East 171st Street, Westfield, IN 46074, are open Monday through Friday 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. and closed from noon to 1 p.m.; the Building Division lists 317-804-3150, extension 5, and building@westfield.in.gov. Westfield has a page devoted to roofing questions. Its Roofing FAQs page says no permit is required to replace shingles or to replace a roof, that the work must still meet the current Indiana Residential Code, and that "Roofing materials must be installed in accordance with the manufacturer's installation instructions." It adds that the city sets no ice and water shield requirement beyond the state code, that shield must go on if the maker's instructions require it, and that ignoring those instructions is treated as a code violation. The Building Division page says all permit applications are submitted through the City's Citizens Portal.

The residential single-family permit page says nothing about contractor registration, so this draft makes no statement about whether Westfield registers or licenses roofers. Ask the Building Division.

What Westfield's Building Division page says about the permit process

The Building Division page describes a portal workflow rather than a counter visit. Applicants use the Citizens Portal to track an application's status, to request inspections and to read the results, and the page puts the burden of asking for an inspection on the applicant, who must also make sure the site can be reached during the scheduled inspection window. It states that fees must be completed, along with all required inspections, approvals and documentation, before a Certificate of Occupancy is released, and it points to a separate Fee Schedule page. The Building Division page lists no contractor requirements, gives no fee amounts and does not say how far ahead an inspection must be requested, so those are three more questions for building@westfield.in.gov or 317-804-3150.

Westfield's historic preservation rules

Westfield's city code has a subchapter that establishes a Historic Preservation Commission, and its definitions section, 33.131, sets the vocabulary. A historic district can be a single property or a larger grouping, with its boundaries shown on a map that the City Council adopts by ordinance. Primary areas hold the main historic or architectural significance, and secondary areas are adjacent zones that must stay compatible with them. Properties are rated Outstanding, Notable, Contributing or Non-contributing, and a Contributing property is one at least 40 years old.

Two definitions matter to a homeowner. An alteration is a material or color change in the external architectural features of a property in a historic district, and routine maintenance is work for which no certificate of appropriateness is required. The definitions section does not mention roofs and does not say what counts as routine, so this page does not claim that a reroof is or is not routine. The Building Division's roofing page, quoted above, says no permit is needed to replace shingles, which answers the building permit question only. For a house in or beside a mapped district, ask the Building Division at building@westfield.in.gov whether any preservation step applies as well.

Roofing licenses in Indiana

Roofing has no entry on the Indiana Professional Licensing Agency's profession list, which does name plumbing, real estate and home inspectors. The Attorney General's storm-chaser leaflet says "Licensing requirements vary from community to community." In Westfield, the city's own page says a permit is not required for a reroof, and the remaining question is the contractor's local status.

Questions for your Westfield bids

- Ask each bidder whether the quote follows the shingle maker's written installation instructions, since the city treats that as a code matter.

- Ask whether the maker's instructions call for ice and water shield on your roof, since the state table says "No" for Hamilton County.

- Ask the Building Division whether the contractor needs to be registered or licensed for your job.

- Ask whether the quote covers replacing damaged decking and how that is priced, since the city's roofing page speaks only to shingles and the roof as a whole.

- Show each bidder the same copy of any insurer estimate in writing.
